entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
James Justinian Morier (c. 1780 – 19 March 1849) was a British diplomat and author whose literary works, particularly *The Adventures of Hajji Baba of Ispahan*, provided a foundational, albeit often Orientalist, portrayal of early 19th-century Qajar Iran to a Western audience. His diplomatic service in Persia between 1808 and 1816, alongside figures like Sir Harford Jones Brydges and Sir Gore Ouseley, granted him unique insights into Persian court life, culture, and Anglo-Persian relations during a period of intense geopolitical maneuvering between the British, Russian, and French empires. His novels, blending satire and ethnographic detail, significantly shaped European perceptions of the Middle East for generations.

Born in Smyrna (modern Izmir, Ottoman Empire) around 1780 to Isaac Morier, a Swiss-British merchant and consul-general, James Justinian Morier embarked on his diplomatic career in 1808 as private secretary to Sir Harford Jones Brydges on a special mission to the Qajar court of Fath-Ali Shah in Tehran. He served as secretary of legation under Sir Gore Ouseley from 1810 to 1814, playing a role in negotiating the Treaty of Gulistan (1813) and the subsequent Treaty of Tehran (1814), which defined Anglo-Persian alliances against Russia. His extensive travels throughout Persia, observing its social strata from nomadic tribes to urban bazaars, provided the rich material for his later literary output. Following his diplomatic retirement in 1817, he published *A Journey through Persia, Armenia, and Asia Minor* (1812) and *A Second Journey through Persia* (1818), which were acclaimed travelogues before he turned to fiction.
